text: Electroplating is a core technology in high-end chip manufacturing, with its technical challenges centered on achieving voidfree filling of metal coatings within micro- and nanoscale trenches and vias. Copper, the current mainstream interconnect material, can no longer meet the performance and reliability demands posed by the continuous reduction in interconnect dimensions. In contrast, cobalt ofers superior electrical properties and safety at the micro-/nanoscale, making it a promising next-generation interconnect material to replace copper. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of cobalt interconnect technology in chip manufacturing. It examines the electrochemical behavior and interactions of cobalt ions, boric acid, and additives, summarizing the cobalt filling efects and associated mechanism models under diferent process compositions. The discussion also highlights advanced in situ electrochemical characterization technologies to investigate the synergistic and antagonistic efects of various plating bath components, the influence of pH, temperature, and additives on cobalt nucleation and growth, and the surface, interface, and filling processes during cobalt electrodeposition in micro-/nanostructures. Furthermore, the paper explores annealing treatments for cobalt coatings, emphasizing their role in optimizing performance.

text: The rapid advancement of electronic information and technology has significantly enhanced living standards, driven scientific and technological innovation, and promoted social progress. At the heart of electronic information and technology lies the design, manufacturing, and testing of chips. Electroplating plays a pivotal role in the fabrication, integration, and packaging of integrated circuit chips. It is the only technology capable of achieving nanoscale electronic logic interconnects and enabling the large-scale, controllable manufacturing of metal-based micro-/nanostructures. 1–6 Furthermore, electroplating serves as a foundation for semiconductor chip interconnects and holds promise for the future integration and packaging of carbon-based, biological, and quantum chips.

text: Copper has high resistance to electromigration and excellent thermal and electrical conductivity, so it is the main metal material for electrical interconnects, 7–17 as shown in Fig. 1. However, with the rapid development of integrated circuit industry, the wiring density and metal layer stacking continually increase, e.g., the length of the chip internal metal wiring has been up to tens of kilometers, and the number of the metal wiring layers is up to 15. The improvement in energy consumption and performance requires the size of transistors and metal interconnects to shrink continuously, with the resulting size efects. The more significant grain boundary scattering and interface scattering of electrons inside the metal caused by size efects are shown in Fig. 2.13 When the width of copper interconnects line decreases, the current load increases sharply, then the resistivity increases sharply, which will damage the chip performance due to the serious resistance and capacitance delay and a large amount of Joule heat. Therefore, copper interconnects have been unable to meet the development needs of advanced integrated circuit in the post-Moore era, and it is urgent to find next-generation metal interconnect materials.

text: The electron mean free path of copper is 39 nm. 18 Generally, the larger the electron mean free path of the bulk metal, the lower the resistivity of the metal. When the characteristic size of interconnects is reduced to the electron mean free path of copper, the electrons inside the copper are subjected to strong grain boundary scattering and interface scattering, causing a sudden increase in resistivity. Compared with copper, cobalt has a smaller electron mean free path (about 10 nm); 18 that is, cobalt possesses a smaller size efect than copper. 19 When the trench critical dimension is above about 7 nm, copper wires have lower resistivity. When the trench critical dimension is below about 7 nm, cobalt wires exhibit even lower resistivity. 20 The resistivities of diferent widths for Cu and Co are shown in Fig. 3. In addition, in copper interconnects, the TiN barrier layer and copper seed layer with about 2 nm thickness in total are needed to prevent the interdifusion of copper and dielectric Si / SiO _ 2, which further reduces the width of copper interconnect line, resulting in a higher resistivity. Cobalt itself can act as a barrier layer or seed layer. 21 Theoretically, using cobalt as interconnect metal does not require a barrier layer and a seed layer with higher resistivity, thereby further improving the conductivity of the interconnect metal. Although cobalt has better electromigration resistance than copper, in practice, if a barrier layer is not used, cobalt will still difuse into the SiO _ 2 dielectric layer or porous low-K dielectric layer. 22 In the absence of an seed layer or barrier layer, cobalt will also difuse into the trench of other layers along the interface of the filling layer/dielectric layer. 23 Cobalt is an ideal next-generation interconnected metal material to replace copper.

text: A cobalt electroplating bath is mainly composed of virgin make-up solution (VMS) and organic additives. The VMS consists of cobalt sulfate heptahydrate ( CoSO _4·7H_2 O), boric acid (H _ 3 BO _ 3), cobalt chloride hexahydrate ( CoCl _2·6H_2 O) and sulfuric acid (H_2 SO _ 4).. Table I presents the composition of the VMS. 29–31 CoSO _4·7H_2O is the metal source of cobalt electrodeposition. If the content of cobalt ions is too high, the surface roughness of coating will increase. In contrast, if the content is too small, it is easy to produce intermediate inclusions and surface defects of the coating ^ 2 9 CoCl _2·6H_2O can provide chloride ions. On the one hand, they can promote the dissolution of cobalt anode during electroplating, while, on the other hand, they can cooperate with organic additives to change the cobalt reaction process. 30 ^-32H_2 SO _ 4 regulates the pH value of the electroplating solution to 3–4 and prevents the electrodeposited cobalt layer from passiva tion and formation of Co ( OH) _ 2, which makes the reaction dificult to continue. Since the reduction potential of cobalt is more negative than that of hydrogen, the hydrogen evolution reaction often occurs simultaneously with the cobalt ions electro-reduction during cobalt electroplating. To avoid a large change in the local pH value, it is often necessary to add a pH bufering agent to maintain a constant pH value. H_3 BO _ 3,, as a pH bufering agent, can prevent the pH changes caused by hydrogen evolution reactions. Organic additives are the key components to achieve cobalt bottomup superfilling. 33–38

text: Rigsby et al. 39 found that H_3 BO _ 3 could refine grain and reduce coating roughness, as shown in Fig. 6. Furthermore, when the content of H_3 BO _ 3 was too low, the trenches were sealed in advance, leaving many holes and gaps, as displayed in Fig. 7. The H_3 BO _ 3 plays a relatively complex role in cobalt electroplating interconnects. During the cobalt electroplat ing process, due to the continuous occurrence of the hydrogen evolution reaction, the pH value of the local electrolyte near the cathode surface increases significantly. The H_3 BO _ 3 must be converted into polyborates and the released H ^ + ions will reduce the local pH value and hinder the formation of Co ( OH) _ 2 near the cathode surface. 40 In addition, polyborates are easily adsorbed on the cathode surface, occupying active sites for atomic hydrogen electro-reduction and inhibiting the hydrogen evolution reaction. 41 Generally, most chemical substances are adsorbed on the electrode surface, which can inhibit the electrodeposition of metal ions. However, as the concentration of H_3 BO _ 3 increases, the adsorbed polyborate results in an increase in the current utilization rate of cobalt electrodeposition. 39 That is to say, the mechanism of converting H_3 BO _ 3 into polyborates on the cathode surface, the mechanism of inhibiting the reduction of atomic hydrogen, the types of polyborates adsorbed on the cathode surface and their adsorption modes, and the mechanism of polyborates capturing metal ions to form complexes to improve current utilization are currently inconclusive. Research on H_3 BO _ 3 in cobalt electroplating interconnects is still in its preliminary stage and there is room for discussion on the mechanism, but what is certain is that H_3 BO _ 3 plays an indispensable role in cobalt electroplating from three aspects: stabilizing the pH, inhibiting surface hydrogen evolution, and promoting cobalt electrodeposition for high current utilization.

raw: Additives and Superfilling Mechanism

text: Metal cobalt is an iron group element, so the additives suitable for electroplating of iron group metals can be used for cobalt electroplating. Alkynol/enol compounds (including sulfonated compounds) are typical additives for cobalt electrodeposition. The molecular structure is shown in Fig. 8. However, to date, there are almost no reports on the use of alkynol/enol compounds for bottom-up superfilling of cobalt, and only a few studies have explored their reaction process on the surface of cobalt electrodes. Jin et al. 42 showed the molecule structure, adsorption ability, and electrochemical property of butynediol. Pan et al. 43 believed that the electrodeposited cobalt can catalyze the occurrence of the hydrogen evolution reaction, and the atomic hydrogen produced continuously reduced butynediol adsorbed on the cobalt electrode surface. Kiruba et al. 36 reported that butynediol can be reduced to butenediol on the cobalt electrode surface in the electroplating bath through Raman spectroscopy. In addition, there was electrochemical oscillation behavior in the initial stage of cobalt electrodeposition due to the three reasons of the interaction between atomic hydrogen and butynediol adsorption, the reaction between atomic hydrogen and butynediol, and the cobalt ions electro-reduction. Although there are no reports on the use of alkynol/ enol compounds for cobalt bottom-up superfilling, this does not mean that alkynol/enol compounds cannot achieve cobalt bottom-up superfilling without voids. If these alkynol/enol compounds can control the rate of cobalt electrodeposition at the bottom of the via to be higher than that at the mouth, then these alkynol/enol compounds are suitable additives and meet the requirements of bottom-up superfilling.

text_index: Difusion Dependent and Induction-Difusion- Adsorption Mechanism
raw: Difusion‑Dependent and Induction–Difusion– Adsorption Mechanism

text: Dye additives are usually nitrogen-containing compounds, which are often regarded as levelers and applied to copper electroplating interconnects. 45–54 Dye additives have the characteristics of inhibiting metal electrodeposition and difusion dependence, so they can also be used for cobalt electroplating interconnects. Nitrotetrazolyl blue (NBT) and malachite green (MG) are the typical dye-type additives for cobalt electroplating, and their corresponding structures are shown in Fig. 10a. Li et al. 31 showed that NBT has a concentration gradient in the trench structure. As cobalt electrodeposition proceeds, the NBT content at the bottom of the trench is lower than that at the mouth, and therefore cobalt can be filled from bottom to top. Figure 10b shows the proposed difusion-dependent mechanism for cobalt bottom-up superfilling based on the NBT action mechanism. It is worth noting that, unlike copper electroplating, the bottom-up superfilling mechanism of cobalt electroplating is also related to the atomic hydrogen concentration on the electrode surface in addition to the type of additives. Some dye additives can promote the occurrence of the hydrogen evolution reaction, which afects the bottom-up superfilling efect by changing the cobalt electrodeposition current eficiency. Ma et al. 55 believed that MG can promote the generation of atomic hydrogen. There was a concentration gradient of MG in the trench, and the MG concentration was high at the trench mouth. At the same time, MG promoted the occurrence of the hydrogen evolution reaction at the trench mouth, resulting in a decrease in the current eficiency of cobalt electrodeposition there. In contrast, the current eficiency of cobalt electrodeposition at the bottom of the trench was high. Therefore, cobalt was densely superfilled from bottom to top. Based on this characteristic, an induction–dif fusion–adsorption mechanism suitable for cobalt bottom-up superfilling was proposed, as shown in Fig. 10c.

text: The above-mentioned cobalt bottom-up superfilling mechanism is closely related to the kinds of additives, but there are also some mechanisms that do not limit the kinds of additives, such as the diferential current eficiency fill (DCEF) mechanism. Rigsby et al. 56–58 considered that the local pH changes directly afected the concentration of hydroxide ions involved in the formation of intermediates, Co(OH)_ads, thereby increasing the reaction paths, changing the thermodynamics of cobalt electrodeposition, and adjusting the rate of cobalt electrodeposition. They confirmed that there was a concentration gradient of hydrogen ions in the via (high concentration at the mouth of via), and the current eficiency of cobalt electrodeposition at the bottom of the via was four times higher than that at the mouth by using cyclic voltammetry with electrochemical quartz microbalance technology. The formation of a pH gradient in the longitudinal direction of the via structure led to diferences in the cobalt electrodeposition rate and eficiency, which enabled bottom-up superfilling. Based on the experimental results, the DCEF mechanism was proposed and is shown in Fig. 11.

text: Another mechanism that is not afected by the types of additives is the hydrogen reduction-induced deactivation (HID) mechanism. Wu et al. 59,60 verified that the change of pH value afected the inhibiting ability of additives through cyclic voltammetry. During the cobalt electrodeposition process, a large amount of atomic hydrogen accumulates at the bottom of the via due to the large surface-to-volume ratio, and the inhibitor at the bottom of via is continuously protonated and loses the ability to inhibit the electro-reduction of cobalt ions. A schematic of the HID mechanism is presented in Fig. 12. According to the principles described in this mechanism, any additive that undergoes a transition between an inactive state and active state under the influence of hydrogen ions can control and achieve the cobalt bottomup superfilling.

text: Nucleation and Growth
text_index: Nucleation and Growth
raw: Nucleation and Growth

text: The nucleation and growth process of cobalt interconnect wires has a huge impact on their stability and resistivity. Pagnanelli et al. 70 found that increasing the overpotential of cobalt electrodeposition will increase the number of active sites on the surface, resulting in an increase in the density of cobalt nuclei and a significant decrease in grain size. Mehmood et al. 71 confirmed that the overpotential of cobalt electrodeposition is closely related to its growth structure. High overpotential is conducive to the formation of facecentered cubic cobalt clusters with a small core radius. In addition, pH has an efect on the nucleation of micron-scale cobalt, but has no efect on the nucleation of nanoscale cobalt. 72 Mukhtar et al. 73 showed that the concentration of cobalt ion has a significant efect on its nucleation. When the concentration is low, the cobalt nucleus is larger and the structure is hexagonal close-packed. As the concentration is high, the cobalt nucleus is smaller and the structure is facecentered cubic. A schematic is shown in Fig. 13.

text: The phenomenon that an autocatalytic reaction causes a positive feedback loop is regard as electrochemical oscillation. 75–78 The self-adsorption/desorption, decomposition and competitive adsorption of additives on the electrode surface may change the kinetic mechanism of metal ion electro-reduction, resulting in electrochemical oscillation, and periodic changes in current or potential within a certain range. 78–81 Numerous studies on electrochemical oscillation for copper interconnects have been reported, 82–85 but, to the best of our knowledge, only one report on the electrochemical oscillation of cobalt interconnects has been published. Hu et al. 86 reported that 3-mercapto-1-propanesulfonate (MPS) can lead to an electrochemical oscillation. The main positive feedback loops resulting in oscillation are autocatalytic accumulation and dissolution of cobalt hydroxide, which are triggered by the potential-dependent adsorption and desorption of the Co-MPS complex. Figure 15 shows the potential oscillation phenomen0n and mechanism of cobalt.

text: Additive molecules can coordinate metal ions on the electrode surface, thereby changing the electrode process kinetics of metal deposition. BNS also transforms the nucleation of cobalt from instantaneous nucleation to progressive nucleation, result ing in a more uniform and dense cobalt film morphology. The selectivity and strong adsorption of BNS on the cobalt plane are the reasons for the preferential orientation growth of the (002) crystal plane. After annealing, the cobalt film prepared by BNS had obvious grain growth, obvious impurity difusion, and further improved electrical properties. Su et al. 95 showed that the hardness of nanocrystalline Co coatings increases with the decrease of grain size. Small average grain sizes and smooth surfaces contribute to the improvement of corrosion resistance of the coatings. A coating obtained by reverse pulse electrodeposition had the finest grains, the highest hardness, and the highest corrosion resistance, followed by bipolar pulse electrodeposition. Hardness, surface roughness, morphology, and phase structure have significant efects on the tribological properties and wear mechanism of nanocrystalline Co coatings, with those prepared by dual pulse electrodeposition showing the highest wear resistance and the lowest friction due to their higher hardness and smoothness. Nanocrystalline Co coatings prepared by reverse pulse electrodeposition showed the highest friction and the lowest wear resistance due to their higher surface roughness, the absence of an hcp(110) peak, and the weakening of the hcp(100) peak.

text: At present, the study of cobalt electroplating often obtains average information of various thermodynamics and kinetics of the electrode/solution interface and electrode surface processes at the macrolevel by using classical electrochemical research methods and theoretical calculations. However, classical electrochemical research methods find it dificult to identify the characteristics of electrode reaction intermediates and products, and cannot provide mechanism information at the microscopic and molecular levels. raw: Conclusions

text: Electroplating is a critical technology in high-end electronic manufacturing, including integrated circuits. As interconnect dimensions continue to shrink, copper electroplating is increasingly unable to meet the required performance and safety standards. Cobalt, with its superior electrical properties and safety at the micro-/nanoscale, is emerging as a promising next-generation interconnect material to replace copper. Although there have been reports on cobalt electroplating, current research has primarily focused on the electrochemical behavior of cobalt ions and additives, the role of additives, and the filling efects in trenches and vias, along with proposed filling mechanisms. However, several key aspects remain insuficiently explored. These include the specific actions and synergistic/antagonistic interactions of components such as boric acid and additives in the plating bath, the mechanisms by which pH, temperature, and individual bath components influence cobalt nucleation and growth, and the surface, interface, and filling processes during cobalt electrodeposition in micro-/nanostructures. Future research directions should prioritize the development and application of advanced in situ techniques, including morphological, spectroscopic, and energy spectroscopic, to address these challenges. Clarifying these mechanisms will be essential for advancing cobalt electroplating as a viable interconnect technology in next-generation chip fabrication.
